# redline

Read one Text Artifact against the editorial contract, repair what the review found within the budget the invocation allows, say what is left, and close with one mechanical pass. The artifact may come from anywhere: this collection wrote it, a person wrote it, or something else produced it entirely.

Run `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1 uv run "$HERE/scripts/invoke.py"` — `$HERE` is the directory that holds this SKILL.md — with everything the user typed after `/redline`, verbatim and however many lines, on stdin. Exit 0: do what it prints. On any other exit, if you introduced a known construction error and can correct it while preserving the user's request and authority, account for effects already produced, submit the corrected invocation through the same shim, and continue from the failed boundary; a refusal before the operation starts consumes no operation. Otherwise show what it printed to the user verbatim and stop. Never repair input the user supplied, or automatically retry exact help, an unmet dependency, an unrelated failure, or a failure whose origin or valid correction is unknown.

Run every UV command in this Skill with a fresh private directory as `TMPDIR`, and remove that directory after the command, including when it fails. The private directory belongs to that one command and no other run, so cleanup removes only files this run created.

## Arguments

The operand is the Text Artifact: inline text, one local path, or one URL, and exactly one of them — several paths, a glob reaching more than one file, or a directory of texts is more than one. Where the invocation carries no operand, it is the single text the current turn identifies.

`--genre=<genre>` names a resource under `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/genres/`, by its filename without the extension.

`--technique=<technique>` names a resource under `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/techniques/`, the same way.

`--language=<language>` names the language or locale whose editorial guidance applies. Any spelling the Collection's resolver reaches is accepted — a canonical code (`sv`, `en_GB`), a case or separator variant of one (`en-GB`, `EN_GB`), a curated alias (`BrE`, `brittisk engelska`), or an ordinary description of a language in any language.

`--brief=<path>|<url>` names the Writing Brief to review the text against. It is supplied material, never a Text Artifact: never edit, proofread or deliver it. The brief can also be named by a Contextual Instruction or applicable Conversation Context, as `## Resolution` describes.

`--max=<n>` is the Correction Budget: the greatest number of substantive corrections the review may delegate. It takes any non-negative integer and defaults to `1`, so an ordinary review includes one correction and one opportunity to verify it. `0` reviews without correcting — the findings come back for the reader to act on, and the closing mechanical pass is still performed — and a higher value bounds a longer loop explicitly. It is a ceiling and never a quota: a run with nothing left to correct stops with the rest of it unspent.

`--output=response|<path>` names the Output Target. `response` is the default and the value `response` states it explicitly; anything else is one filesystem path. It and In-place Editing name two destinations for one text, which is why no form carries both.

`--in-place[=<value>]` selects In-place Editing. It accepts `yes`, `on`, and `true` against `no`, `off`, and `false`; bare `--in-place` means `on`, `--in-place=off` has the same effect as omitting the option, and the default is `off`.

## Resolution

Resolve the Writing Brief first: the Formal Invocation's `--brief`, then a Contextual Instruction naming the brief the text is to be reviewed against, then applicable Conversation Context naming it for that review. The map level is empty for this parameter. A value at one level suppresses those below it; where they name different briefs, the delivery names the suppressed instruction and the brief used. Mere presence of a brief in the session, including an earlier `/brief` or `/write` run, selects nothing. Without a pointer at one of these three levels, use no brief and follow the existing contract-only review. With a selected brief, read [`brief-review.md`](references/brief-review.md) before settling the destination or configuration; it governs reading, review, correction and reporting for this branch.

Genre, technique, and language are each resolved on their own, in this order of precedence:

1. The Formal Invocation.
2. A recognized Kntnt map in the selected brief's leading YAML frontmatter, then the Text Artifact's map for each value the brief omits. Where the two maps disagree on genre, technique or language, the brief's map wins below the Formal Invocation and the disagreement is always a finding, even when a flag overrides both. With only one map, use that map as supplied material. A recognized map is in leading YAML frontmatter — the reserved `kntnt` key and its `genre`, `technique`, and `language` values, and nothing else. A `language`, `lang`, `genre`, or `technique` key at the top level of the document's own frontmatter belongs to that document, whatever it is named and whatever it holds; frontmatter carrying no `kntnt` map carries no configuration of this collection's.
3. The current Contextual Instruction.
4. Applicable Conversation Context.
5. Inference from the Text Artifact itself.
6. For the technique alone: the technique the resolved genre names as the one it is ordinarily written with, where that genre names one.
7. The parameter's default: `general` for genre, no technique, and the language of the Text Artifact.

A value found at one level suppresses the levels below it for that parameter alone. An explicit genre beside a language read out of the map and a technique taken from an instruction is an ordinary invocation, not a conflict. Suppression is that precedence working rather than an error: a Contextual Instruction every higher level has already settled leaves nothing for it to settle, and the run continues rather than refusing it as unaddressable guidance. Where saying so is useful, the delivery names the suppressed instruction beside the resolved configuration.

Two things are never inferred. A technique applies because it was selected — by the invocation, the map, an instruction that names one, or the genre that was resolved — and never because the text happens to fall into its shape. A language is settled rather than guessed: where the artifact is materially ambiguous or mixed, with no dominant language or alternation inside paragraphs, name the candidates and ask before anything is reviewed.

A genre inferred rather than named is inferred against what is installed. The genre directory is the list of installed values, and a run inferring one may read a single thing besides that listing: the opening of each installed genre resource — its `# <Name>` heading and the paragraph under it, which every resource carries so that a reader choosing between them has something to read without loading the rest. Read that far and no further. What a genre asks for is not evidence about whether that genre applies, so a resource read past its opening has been loaded rather than considered — and the loading step below is unchanged by any of this: it loads the genre inference settled on, and no other. Where no installed genre fits what is in front of you better than the default does, the default at the foot of the precedence stands.

Level 6 belongs to the technique alone, and it is read after the genre is settled and out of the genre that was settled: that resource's base half names the technique this kind of text is ordinarily written with, or states that it has none, and nothing else is opened for it. What the genre carries there is a selection rather than evidence — an installed genre names its ordinary arc whatever text is in front of you — so a technique reached this way is settled exactly as an instruction naming one settles it, and a genre naming none leaves the level below it standing.

Handoff Metadata is never required and never created. A Text Artifact carrying no `kntnt` map is reviewed exactly like one that carries a complete one, and no map is added to it. Where the Text Artifact has a recognized map, it is used as defaults here and synchronized to the resolved configuration in step 8; the brief's map stays untouched.

`none` for the technique is a value rather than a gap, and it is how the genre's arc is refused. Written in a recognized map it says that the run which wrote the map resolved no technique; said in an instruction or in Conversation Context it says the same thing at that level. Either settles the parameter where it sits, above the genre's level, so the genre supplies nothing and no technique is applied; natural narrative or logical progression remains available. It names no resource, so it is not the uninstalled value the refusal below reaches. `--technique` takes an installed name and has no spelling for this, which is why the levels below the invocation are where it is said.

A recognized Kntnt map whose winning value cannot be used — a language nothing installs, a genre or technique that is not there — is reported as unusable supplied metadata and stops the run, unless the Formal Invocation already settled that parameter. A text-map value suppressed by the brief map remains part of the reported conflict; it does not replace the winning value. It is never quietly read as the nearest usable value, so a spelling such as `en_UK` never becomes `en_GB` on its own.

## Steps

1. Settle the single Text Artifact and the options from the JSON, resolve the optional Writing Brief by `## Resolution`, and confirm that this Harness can start a fresh subagent. Where it cannot, report the Unsatisfied Capability, review nothing, write nothing, and stop. A value outside what `## Arguments` admits — `--max` that is not a non-negative integer, `--in-place` outside its vocabulary, or more than one Text Artifact — is refused as `$LIBRARY/references/invocation-envelope.md` says: review nothing, write nothing, and stop. In a Harness that can start a fresh subagent, that is the whole of what is refused over the invocation, the engine having already held its form: whatever the operand turns out to say, and whatever the review will have to say about it, an invocation the engine read and these values admit is reviewed. A run that finds itself wanting to refuse one has found a gap in the pages rather than a reason to stop — review the invocation, and name the gap beside the findings where it is worth naming. Done when the Capability is confirmed and one Text Artifact and a valid set of options are in hand, or you have stopped.
2. Settle the destination before anything is reviewed, following `$LIBRARY/references/delivery.md`. Make every refusal that contract names by reading alone — In-place Editing together with a separate Output Target, an output path equal to the input path, In-place Editing against inline text or a URL or a source that is not a writable local file, and a destination whose parent directory does not exist — so that a refusal has nothing written behind it. For a selected brief, also refuse any destination that would replace its file, including In-place Editing when the text and brief name the same file; compare resolved paths and file identity, not just their spelling. Done when the destination is settled, or you have stopped.
3. Read the Text Artifact's leading YAML frontmatter where it has any, and look in it for one top-level `kntnt` map. Read `genre`, `technique`, and `language` out of that map and nothing else out of it, and read nothing outside it as configuration. Read the selected brief's map the same way and retain both maps as received for conflict reporting. Done when both documents' recognized values are known to be present, absent, or unusable, or when no brief was selected and the artifact's are known.
4. Resolve genre, technique, and language by `## Resolution`. A genre or technique is verified against the resources actually installed in the two directories named in `## Arguments`; one that is not there is refused as `$LIBRARY/references/invocation-envelope.md` says, and the run reviews nothing, writes nothing, and stops. Where the genre has to be inferred rather than verified, `## Resolution` says what may be read to infer it. Settle the genre before the technique, since the technique's last level reads what the settled genre names. A language selector is verified by `uv run --no-cache --no-project "$LIBRARY/scripts/languages.py" resolve --scope=composition --scope=review --scope=anti-slop "<selector>"`, whose non-zero exit says which of the ways it failed — no installed Language Resource reached, or more than one — and takes that same refusal; an unlisted description of a language is interpreted first, then proposed as one installed candidate and verified through that same command. Report unusable recognized metadata as `## Resolution` describes, and ask rather than guess at a mixed language. Nothing has been written yet, so asking costs nothing to undo. Done when all three are settled, or you have asked or refused.
5. Load what the review is read against, and nothing besides it: `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/base.md` and `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/base.review.md`; the selected genre from `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/genres/` and the `.review.md` file beside it where one exists; the resolved technique from `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/techniques/` and its `.review.md` the same way; `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/anti-slop.md`; and the three language scopes the resolver already returned in step 4. For `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`, and for `webcopy`, also load `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/web-craft.md` and `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/web-craft.review.md`; for `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion` alone, also load `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/article-anatomy.md` and `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/article-anatomy.review.md`, which fix the parts, order and dimensions of such a text; and for those four and for `pressrelease`, also load `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/headlines.md` and `$LIBRARY/references/editorial/headlines.review.md`, which say how a headline and its subheadings are written. These are the only additional genre support files: follow no other genre links and load no unselected genre or technique. A review extension that is not there is not a defect — a base half on its own is a complete resource. Load no mechanics guidance: the mechanical pass in step 9 resolves its own. With a selected brief, also load the Library template and the material `brief-review.md` specifies. Done when those are loaded and nothing else has been.
6. Review the Text Artifact against everything loaded in step 5. Read each passage of reported speech as a review unit against the resolved language and genre guidance, preserving its meaning and distinctive voice; then cover the surrounding prose and the relations between passages. Record findings with the passage, requirement and what the reader loses. A finding against a headline, a standfirst or a subheading names that part and the defect in it — a claim the text does not carry, a heading from which a reader who sees only it cannot tell what the text is about, a subject named with nothing said about it, the opening it repeats — as a finding against any other passage names its defect, since that defect is what the delivery reports a repaired part by. For `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`, the anatomy's counted limits are measured rather than read: run `uv run --no-cache --no-project "$LIBRARY/scripts/article_anatomy.py" -` with the complete Text Artifact on stdin, and take every count a finding reports from that output rather than from your own reading of the text. Exit 0 settles the counted requirements only: it says none of them is a finding, and nothing about the anatomy requirements the script does not count — whether the last section is an ending, whether the standfirst stands on its own, whether a subheading describes its section — which this review examines by reading the text, and step 11 reports the text as conforming to the anatomy only where every one of them was examined; exit 1 makes each requirement it names a finding; exit 2 says the script could not measure the text, so count the limits by hand and say in step 11's delivery that they were not machine-measured. A norm it reports is a finding only where `article-anatomy.review.md` says a departure from a *should* is one, and the `typical` figures it reports feed the whole-text reading that file describes, no single paragraph or section failing one of them. Read every `heading_pairs` entry against the full text and the loaded headline contract, including pairs with no `shared_words`: judge whether the two parts add different information in different wording. Necessary repeated names or topic words alone create no finding; a paraphrased repeat can be a finding with little or no overlap. Verify absent or ambiguous sentence estimates against the text, and inspect the pairs by hand on exit 2. Record a semantic echo with its pair, the headline requirement and what the reader loses, independently of structural conformance and exit status. For `pressrelease`, the two counted limits the genre states are measured the same way, with `--genre=pressrelease` before the `-`, and every count a finding reports comes from that output: exit 0 says neither limit is a finding and settles nothing else of the release, exit 1 makes each limit it names a finding, and exit 2 says the script found no level-1 heading or could not read the text, so count by hand and say in step 11's delivery that the limits were not machine-measured. That output carries no norms, `typical` figures or `heading_pairs`; read the headline and the summary against each other as the genre's review half says. A code sample — a fenced block, an indented block, or an inline code span — is quoted material rather than the text's own prose: its contents are read past rather than read against the rules, so nothing inside one is a finding and nothing inside one is changed, the docstrings, comments, and string literals among them. Prose about code is ordinary prose and is read like every other sentence. Judge only what is in front of you. What the artifact turns out to be is a finding and never a ground for declining to review it: a text that reads as a brief, an outline, or notes rather than a finished piece is reviewed against the resolved genre like any other, and that mismatch is a finding — ordinarily the first one — instead of a reason to stop, to hand the invocation back, or to propose another Skill in its place. Reaching that judgement reads no other Skill's instructions, neither a `SKILL.md` of theirs nor a `help.md`; the mechanical pass in step 9 is the one Skill this run ever follows. Without a selected brief, this Skill never compares the Text Artifact with source material, never asks for material it was not given, and never remarks that source verification was unavailable — Source Fidelity is the contract of the Skill that wrote the text, and a caveat about material nobody supplied is noise in every run that was not one. A contradiction, an unsupported claim, or an editorial defect visible inside the artifact itself is an ordinary finding. With a selected brief, also perform the question-by-question assessment in `brief-review.md` and merge its shortfalls and map conflicts into these findings. Done when the applicable reviews are complete.
7. Spend the Correction Budget, up to it and never towards it. While findings remain from the most recent review and budget remains, take one round:
   - Delegate the correction to a subagent started fresh for this round, from [`correction.md`](references/correction.md), filled in and delivered as that brief says. Fresh means it carries no history: not what an earlier round found, not what an earlier correction attempted, and not your own reading of the text, so the framing of the round before cannot bias this repair. It receives the complete current Text Artifact and the complete findings of the most recent review — the text as it now stands and every finding as it was recorded, never a summary and never a stale draft — the genre, technique, and language resolved in step 4, and the requirement to leave alone everything the findings do not concern.
   - Decrement the budget once per correction, whatever that correction came back with. A round that repaired nothing has still spent what it spent.
   - Retain the complete current text as the pre-round Text Artifact. Before the returned text becomes current, compare it with that pre-round Text Artifact and record every removed claim, whether the finding named that whole claim as the defect or the claim sat beside the defect; every changed claim beside them — a claim that has a counterpart in the pre-round Text Artifact and that the round left standing with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality or meaning moved; and every added claim — one the returned text asserts and the pre-round Text Artifact has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say. A shorter text can be clean against step 6 while having silently lost what the earlier state said, so this comparison is part of re-review rather than an inference from the returned text. Where a claim sat beside the defect, reject the returned correction, keep the pre-round Text Artifact as current, carry the original finding forward as unresolved, and treat the attempted loss as the repair-created finding that stops the loop below. Where the finding named the whole claim as the defect, its removal may stand, but the delivery still names the claim that went. That permission stops at a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts — that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that the text is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Naming the whole of one as the defect licenses nothing: its removal or weakening stands only where the finding named a defect inside it and either another retained sentence still states that limit in full, so the text bounds what it claims exactly as far as it did, or the limit contradicts another passage of the same text. Otherwise reject the returned correction as above. For a brief shortfall, also verify every correction against the source support recorded with its finding, under `brief-review.md`; an unsupported addition or change is a repair-created defect and rejects the round. A changed or added claim no rule above rejects is reported rather than rejected, and the delivery names it.
   - Trace the differences beside that comparison. Go through every difference between the returned text and the pre-round Text Artifact — a heading, a paragraph break, a piece of formatting and a substituted word among them, and not the claims alone — and trace each one to a finding of the review that commissioned this round. A difference traces where it repairs what a finding named, or where that repair necessitates it — agreement after a changed subject, a transition the repair would otherwise break. A difference that traces to neither is not accepted: restore that passage byte for byte from the pre-round Text Artifact, and let the rest of the round stand. Restoring a passage verbatim writes no wording of your own, which is why it is a restoration rather than a rejection of the whole round; it spends no budget and is not a finding, and it puts the passage back rather than carrying anything forward for a person to settle. The claim comparison above, its rejections and the four stop conditions below are unchanged by this, and a difference that traces to a finding is still judged by them.
   - Review the returned text again, from the top, exactly as step 6 reviews and against everything loaded in step 5. Until that review has run the returned text is a correction candidate rather than the current Text Artifact: a correction is verified by review and never accepted on the report of whoever made it, an agent reporting on its own work being the one reader who cannot check it, and what that review establishes is what settles whether the candidate is accepted at all. The findings of this review, and not the subagent's account of what it fixed, are the findings from here on.
   - Establish from those findings whether the round introduced a defect. A finding is repair-created where the passage it names differs from the state before the round that wrote that passage and the requirement it names was not violated there: establish the change and the violated requirement against the states you retain and never from how the finding words itself, so that a preference and a defect the text arrived with and nobody had noticed yet are not attributed to a repair. A part the round changed is where this is established most often — a headline, a standfirst or a subheading that said something else before the round, or stood somewhere else. A finding against what such a part now says is a finding the round created: that a finding commissioned the part does not put what it says beyond this check, and that the text was worse without the part is no reason to keep a defective one. And a finding your own round created is never carried forward as an unresolved finding for a person to settle — it is the run's own work rather than the text's, so the run undoes it. Where a repair-created defect is established, reject the whole round that introduced it, whatever else that round repaired, and restore that round's complete pre-round Text Artifact verbatim as the current text; where the round that introduced it is not the last, restore the state immediately before that round and discard every state built on it. Nothing of a rejected round is kept, and earlier accepted work survives only so far as the restored state holds it. Then stop, as the third condition below says. Establish this before you read the budget: a spent budget is why the loop does not go on and never why a defect a round created is delivered, so the third condition is tested before the fourth. A candidate with no repair-created defect established against it becomes the current Text Artifact, and the loop goes on.

   The loop stops at the first of four conditions, and each ends step 7. It stops when no findings remain, leaving the rest of the budget unspent — a text that is already clean is not corrected again to use up a number. It stops when a correction makes no relevant progress, which is a round whose re-review leaves the findings it was given standing with nothing they named changed: the next round would be the same round, so stop and carry those findings forward, saying which of them are unresolved. It stops when a re-review establishes a finding an earlier round's own repair created — a defect the text did not have when it arrived and one of your rounds put there: a claim asserted more strongly than the text supports, a limit a repair dropped, a heading repeating what it stands over, material a round removed, and anything else the resources loaded in step 5 hold. You hold every state the text has passed through and are the only party that does: the subagent is fresh by design and each review reads the text in front of it, so a loop that has begun to answer for its own work is visible here and nowhere else. Another round would repair what the round before it did, so stop — and the round that put the defect there is rejected rather than delivered with what it wrote, because the restored pre-round state is the text this run delivers and a defect of the run's own making is discarded instead of handed to a reader as something to settle. The findings carried forward are the restored text's own, which are the findings that commissioned the rejected round, every one of them unresolved since nothing that round commissioned was kept; the rejected attempt is reported beside them as an attempt and never as a defect of the text delivered. The round keeps the budget it spent: restoration refunds nothing and spends nothing, and it authorizes no wording of your own, no second attempt at the finding it answered and no correction to make up for what was discarded. Name the repair the new finding followed from, which is the thing a person has to settle. And it stops when the budget is spent with findings left, which carries them forward the same way for a person to finish. Done when one of the four has stopped the loop, or the budget was `0` and there was nothing to spend.
8. Where step 3 found a recognized `kntnt` map in the Text Artifact, synchronize its `genre`, `technique`, and `language` to the values resolved in step 4, writing `none` where no technique was resolved, and change nothing else in the frontmatter. Where the artifact carries no such map, add none. Done when the artifact's metadata, if it has any of ours, says what this run resolved.
9. Invoke the installed Proofread Skill exactly once by following `$HERE/../proofread/SKILL.md`; a Formal Invocation its engine refuses before Proofread starts is not the mechanical pass and consumes neither that pass nor the Correction Budget. Freeze the current complete Text Artifact, including frontmatter, in a private input file and reserve a distinct private output path. Use the Formal Invocation `--language=<resolved> --output=<mechanical-output> <mechanical-input>`, with these exact paths. The shim receives flags and the input path, never artifact contents or YAML. If you introduce a known construction error in that invocation, retain the completed review and correction, preserve the two paths and the resolved language, correct only that construction, submit it through the same shim, and continue this step without asking the user. If any failure may have occurred after Proofread started, establish whether it produced the complete output before continuing; never replay a completed pass, and report an unresolved partial outcome as the obstacle. If the outer Contextual Instruction contains guidance relevant to mechanical correction, append only that guidance after an explicit `--`; otherwise pass no Contextual Instruction. Never forward the genre, the technique, the Correction Budget, or unrelated outer context. Do not perform, select, or apply any mechanical corrections yourself: the nested Skill reads the whole input and owns the whole mechanical pass. Verify that the input remains unchanged and read the complete output file as the sole final Text Artifact, including when Proofread reports no change. If the pass cannot complete or its complete result is unavailable, report the obstacle and stop without delivering a purportedly finished artifact. Clean these private files before returning, on every exit. Done when one mechanical pass has produced the complete final artifact.
10. Change nothing substantive after step 9. The mechanical pass is last so that its corrections cannot be undone by later editing, and a sentence improved here would put mechanical errors back into a text that was just cleaned of them. Done when nothing has been touched since the pass.
11. Deliver by `$LIBRARY/references/delivery.md`. With a selected brief, include the brief-fulfilment section required by `brief-review.md`, even when the artifact is unchanged and the ordinary delivery is only a no-change status; the rest of this step still governs the findings and claim account. On a response target, remove every artifact or scratch file this run created and base the delivery account on the filesystem state that remains after cleanup. Say what the review resolved, and where a technique was resolved say where it came from, naming the genre where the genre supplied it, so that somebody who named none can see why an arc was applied; the no-change status carries that too and stays as short as it is. Say that the text conforms to the article anatomy, with or without deviation, only where the review examined every anatomy requirement the script does not count as well as those it counts. Exit 0 settles the counted requirements only, so where one of the others was not examined, name it rather than report conformance. Where findings remain — those step 7 carried forward, whichever of its conditions stopped the loop — deliver the Text Artifact to its Output Target and report the findings separately, saying which are unresolved; the shared delivery contract determines whether an unchanged artifact is repeated or written for each destination. Every headline, standfirst and subheading the text you deliver changed is reported among the findings with the finding its repair answered — the part, and the defect that licensed the change — whether or not any finding remains, so that a reader of the account can tell a repaired part from a rewritten one: a part reported only as rewritten, shortened or reworded says what the run did and not why it was allowed to. Where any round removed a passage carrying a claim, whether an accepted repair removed the claim as the defect or a rejected repair attempted to take it beside the defect, report every removed claim separately and say which repair removed or attempted to remove it; and where a repair took a limit, a connective or a bounding clause out of the text you deliver — a sentence or a heading saying what is not measured, not claimed or not known, a connective giving the text's own reason for what follows, a clause saying what a claim is not about — say what a reader of that text no longer has, however little of the text went with it, since naming the passage says what went and not what the reader lost. Where any round left a claim standing with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality or meaning moved, report every changed claim the same way, saying what it now asserts rather than how far its wording moved, and say which repair moved it, whether or not that round removed anything: a headline, a standfirst and a subheading carry claims like any other passage, so one a round shortened is reported by what it now asserts, never as shorter. Where any round added a claim — one the text you deliver asserts and the text as it arrived has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say — report every added claim the same way, as a class of its own beside the removed and the changed, and say which repair added it — a headline, a standfirst or a subheading a round rewrote is where one is written most often. This account accompanies a clean artifact too, so what the run did to the claims is visible without a diff, and it is an account of the text you deliver rather than of the text you received, a claim the run wrote being as much its business as one that arrived. Every entry of the account describes what happened to its claim as the comparison shows it: a claim a round copied to a second place is not one it moved, and a heading a round reworded with a word of its own is a changed claim wherever that word says more or less than the passage under it. Anything the reply says about the claims as a whole — that none was removed, changed or added, or that nothing else happened to them — is written after the findings and the itemised account, is true of the delivered text, and excepts by name every claim they report; it never contradicts a finding the same reply states, an entry of the account or a sentence of the closing paragraph, and a sentence that could only be written by contradicting one of them is left out. # Tallmora Energi öppnar solpark med 12 000 paneler i gammal grustäkt

Tallmora Energi AB inviger den 3 juni 2027 en solpark vid Kvarnbacken i Tallmora, på marken där kommunens grustäkt låg fram till 2019. Parken har 12 000 solpaneler och beräknas ge 7,5 gigawattimmar el om året.

”Solparken visar att en gammal grustäkt kan göra nytta igen. Vi tror att fler kommuner kommer att pröva samma lösning”, säger Maria Ekholm, vd för Tallmora Energi.

Parken ligger på 18 hektar och har kostat 64 miljoner kronor att bygga. Enligt bolagets beräkning motsvarar årsproduktionen hushållselen i omkring 1 500 villor. Siffran är en uppskattning, och den verkliga produktionen beror på hur soligt året blir.

Elen levereras till elnätet och säljs inte direkt till hushållen i närheten. Området är inhägnat och inte öppet för allmänheten, utom vid invigningen den 3 juni klockan 14.00–16.00, då bolaget visar parken för besökare.

”Vi vill att elen som används i Tallmora också ska produceras här, och Kvarnbacken är det första steget dit”, säger Johan Berg, styrelseordförande i Tallmora Energi.

Grustäkten vid Kvarnbacken avvecklades 2019. Tallmora Energi fick tillstånd att bygga solparken 2025, och bygget började i augusti 2026.

# Press release

An announcement written for the editor deciding whether there is a story here and for the journalist who may take facts from it and publish them. It is not written for the public: it is written for the person standing between an organisation and the public, and it works when they can do their job from it without ringing to ask what something meant.

Write the headline as [Headlines](../headlines.md) says, within the limit below.

## What this genre asks for

**A recipient meets the parts in the order they expect them.** An editor works through many releases in a day and reads each one by habit, finding the next thing where the last release had it, so a release that rearranges the parts spends that habit before its facts get a hearing. A headline and a summary come first and work as a news item together, so that a recipient who reads no further has still been told the news. A short quotation follows the summary, saying what somebody makes of the news. The body comes next and can be facts alone, because the comment has already been made, and a second quotation after it carries one of the most important messages the sender wants the recipient to take away. Then comes what serves the recipient rather than the story: background they may use or leave, the links and attachments that go with the release, the contact details, and last of all a standing description of the organisation. A release owes no heading announcing each part: a recipient finds each one by where it stands.

**The headline states the news on one line.** The headline is the release's level-1 heading (`h1` in HTML, `#` in Markdown). The headline is at most 70 characters, spaces included. It interests an editor by the news it states and never by a word louder than that news: a figure that carries the news belongs in it, and a word of praise, excitement or urgency does not. A time from which the release may be published, where the material states one, stands on a line of its own above the headline, never between the headline and the summary.

**The summary tells the news in full.** The summary is the first paragraph after the headline. The summary is at most 60 words. It names the organisation sending the release and says what has happened or will happen, so that a journalist can copy the headline and the summary into a news item and publish it. A dateline, where the release carries one, opens that paragraph rather than standing as a paragraph of its own. The summary restates the headline's news in full, in its own words, and adds the sender and the particulars: a reader who has just read the headline meets the same news told fully, and never the headline's wording said again. The rule in [Headlines](../headlines.md) that a headline and what follows say different things in different words therefore holds here for the words and the detail and not for the news, since the two together are the notice.

**The news is in the first sentence.** The summary opens with what has happened or will happen, who is doing it, and when. That sentence and the headline above it are the only ones an editor is certain to read, and an opening that describes the organisation, sets a scene, or announces that an announcement is being made has spent them on nothing.

**Every fact is in a form that can be printed.** Dates in full, times and opening hours as they will appear, amounts with their currency and the period they cover, counts as counts, names with the roles that make them relevant, and places spelled as the recipient spells them. A recipient should be able to lift any fact straight into their own text and be right.

**What the announcement excludes is said.** Where a reader would reasonably assume something the material rules out — that a service does a thing it does not do, that a figure covers more than it covers, that a trial is a permanent arrangement — the release says so plainly and once. A sentence costs less than the correction it prevents.

**A quotation is a person saying something only they could say.** Where the material carries an attributed quotation, it appears with the speaker's name and the role that entitles them to what they are saying. Where the material carries none, none is written; a manufactured sentence of enthusiasm is the first thing an editor deletes and the first sign that the rest may be padded too. A quotation carries what somebody makes of the news — an interpretation, a conclusion, a view, a message — and never a fact or a figure of its own: a fact the news depends on stands in the summary or the body, where a journalist can lift it without the quotation marks.

**Each quotation has its place.** The first stands directly after the summary: it is short, comments on the news, draws a conclusion from it and takes a view. The second stands after the body and carries one of the most important messages the sender wants a recipient to take away, and no new fact or figure. Where the material carries one quotation, the release carries that one, directly after the summary, and it carries the message where the material gives it one. Where the material carries two and neither carries a message, each stands in its place as the material gives it, and no message is written into either. Where the material carries none, the release has no quotation, and the gap is the material's: said, never filled.

**The body is one or two short paragraphs.** They complement and deepen the summary, and they are neutral enough that a journalist can lift them straight into their own text without rewriting the substance.

**It reads as information rather than as selling.** The recipient's job is to be sceptical of it, and prose that argues for its subject invites exactly the scepticism the facts then have to survive. What survives is what the material supports and the recipient can check.

**What the release ends with is the material's.** The background carries what a journalist may use and may just as well leave out, so nothing the news depends on is left to it. The links and attachments are what accompanies the release — images, pages on the web, documents — named or linked, and nothing written about them. The contact is a named person a journalist can turn to with further questions: their name, their title, a telephone number and an email address, as far as the material gives them; a name by itself is not a contact. The standing description is a short, factual and neutrally worded account of what the organisation does, written for a journalist's use, and it stops there. Where the material gives nothing for one of these parts, or gives only some of a contact's details, the release goes without what is missing rather than with something written to fill the place.

**It is short.** A release is a page and not a document. Detail beyond what the news needs goes into the background or is left for the recipient to ask about.

## What this genre does not do

It does not write the journalist's article for them, and it does not narrate. Background, colour, and interpretation are theirs to add or leave out; what the release owes them is the news, the facts in a usable form, and somebody to ask.

It adds no requirement the base contract already holds. Register, structure, sentences, words, claims, openings, endings, formatting, and consistency are stated there once, and a rule repeated here would be one rule made into two things to keep true.

## The technique this genre is ordinarily written with

None. The order of the parts above is the whole of a release's structure, and it is a recipient's habit rather than an arc: the news, what somebody makes of it, the facts to lift, and the message the sender stands behind. An arc built over it would take the news off the first sentence, which is the one thing a release cannot spend.

Write the headline as [Headlines](../headlines.md) says, within the limit below.

**A recipient meets the parts in the order they expect them.** An editor works through many releases in a day and reads each one by habit, finding the next thing where the last release had it, so a release that rearranges the parts spends that habit before its facts get a hearing. A headline and a summary come first and work as a news item together, so that a recipient who reads no further has still been told the news. A short quotation follows the summary, saying what somebody makes of the news. The body comes next and can be facts alone, because the comment has already been made, and a second quotation after it carries one of the most important messages the sender wants the recipient to take away. Then comes what serves the recipient rather than the story: background they may use or leave, the links and attachments that go with the release, the contact details, and last of all a standing description of the organisation. A release owes no heading announcing each part: a recipient finds each one by where it stands.

**The headline states the news on one line.** The headline is the release's level-1 heading (`h1` in HTML, `#` in Markdown). The headline is at most 70 characters, spaces included. It interests an editor by the news it states and never by a word louder than that news: a figure that carries the news belongs in it, and a word of praise, excitement or urgency does not. A time from which the release may be published, where the material states one, stands on a line of its own above the headline, never between the headline and the summary.

**The summary tells the news in full.** The summary is the first paragraph after the headline. The summary is at most 60 words. It names the organisation sending the release and says what has happened or will happen, so that a journalist can copy the headline and the summary into a news item and publish it. A dateline, where the release carries one, opens that paragraph rather than standing as a paragraph of its own. The summary restates the headline's news in full, in its own words, and adds the sender and the particulars: a reader who has just read the headline meets the same news told fully, and never the headline's wording said again. **The news is in the first sentence.** The summary opens with what has happened or will happen, who is doing it, and when. That sentence and the headline above it are the only ones an editor is certain to read, and an opening that describes the organisation, sets a scene, or announces that an announcement is being made has spent them on nothing.

**Every fact is in a form that can be printed.** Dates in full, times and opening hours as they will appear, amounts with their currency and the period they cover, counts as counts, names with the roles that make them relevant, and places spelled as the recipient spells them. A recipient should be able to lift any fact straight into their own text and be right.

**What the announcement excludes is said.** Where a reader would reasonably assume something the material rules out — that a service does a thing it does not do, that a figure covers more than it covers, that a trial is a permanent arrangement — the release says so plainly and once. **It is short.** A release is a page and not a document. Detail beyond what the news needs goes into the background or is left for the recipient to ask about.

It does not write the journalist's article for them, and it does not narrate. Background, colour, and interpretation are theirs to add or leave out; what the release owes them is the news, the facts in a usable form, and somebody to ask.

None. # The base contract

Write with the clarity and factual precision of a well-edited newspaper or quality magazine. Genre, audience, and purpose override that register: a letter, a speech and an advertisement keep their own character. The selected genre governs craft and form; the resolved language governs idiom, syntax and typography. Examples here illustrate meanings, not English phrases to translate.

## Reader and progression

Give the intended reader what they need to understand, judge or do the thing the text is for. Keep a clear focus, introduce unfamiliar concepts before the reasoning needs them, and order material by that reader's needs rather than the writer's discovery process. Relevant technical detail belongs; unexplained jargon and unrelated background do not.

Make the relations between passages real. A transition may explain a connection, but cannot invent one. Keep paragraphs coherent and give supporting material a clear place beside what it supports. The body and its sections remain intelligible without treating a title, standfirst or subheading as their opening sentence.

# Headlines

How a headline is written, in any genre that links this file. A headline lets the reader judge at once whether the text is for them: it states the core of the text as briefly and precisely as it can, and it is understood on its own, with no image, standfirst or surrounding page to explain it. *Headline* here covers a text's subheadings too; for a subheading, the text is its section.

## Statement or label

A text that reports, explains, argues, decides or narrates gets a statement headline: a clause that says what the text says. A text the reader looks things up in or navigates by — a policy, a manual, opening hours, a contact page — gets a plain label naming what it holds: *Privacy policy*, where a statement would read *How we protect your data*. Everything below is about the statement headline.

## What a statement headline does

- It states the angle: the single most important message, the sentence that would remain if only one could. A subject alone is a label. Test: the headline could not head a different text on the same subject.
- It is a simple clause — subject, active verb, object where there is one — in straight word order, and in the present tense where that fits: *Council introduces free bus travel*.
- The most important keyword comes first.
- A concrete detail stands in it when the detail carries the message: a number, a date, a place. *Three schools to close this autumn* beats *Changes to school organisation*.
- The reader sees what they gain: a decision, a fact, a change. An instructional text may address the reader directly (*you*, *your*) and open on *How to*, *Why* or *Here's*.
- It is as short as the angle allows. Modifiers, repetition and filler go; a keyword that carries meaning stays. The format the text follows sets the limits.
- It sounds like something a person would say aloud.
- Its words are ones this audience knows. A technical term is the right keyword for specialists and noise for a general reader, and the same holds for names and abbreviations.
- Its tone is the text's tone, and never louder. Illness, accidents, crime and crises get a sober, understated headline; a light text can carry more personality.
- It is plain before it is clever. It works in full for a reader who misses every allusion, so a pun or a reference never carries the meaning.
- It gives the answer. Journalists hold a question headline to be the wrong form, and so does this: it is a deliberate exception, natural over a text built as questions and answers, and available where the text truly leaves the question open and the headline is meant to assert nothing.
- The verb does the work. A colon standing in for a verb, a clipped quotation and headline-speak all give way to the full clause.
- It complements what follows. Headline and standfirst, or subheading and the first sentence under it, say different things in different words.

## Every word supported

A headline claims only what its text claims. Every figure, name, claim and conclusion in it is in the text, at the text's own strength: never sharper, never more general, never a conclusion the text does not draw. A reader who finishes the text finds that the headline told the truth about it.

## A subheading over a quotation

A quotation in a section is there to carry what only its speaker can say: a judgement, a figure, a concession. A subheading standing over it, however far down the section the quotation stands, leaves that to the quotation. It states the section's angle from what the rest of the section says, or, where the quotation is the section's point, names the subject, the occasion or the speaker the quotation speaks to, and not the point itself. Test: a reader who has just read the subheading meets the quotation as new material, never as the subheading said again. *The clinic would double its training time*, over a head nurse saying *Next time I would double the training time before we switch*, has spent the quotation before the reader reaches it; *The head nurse looks back on the switch* leaves it to her.

The quotation bridge is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. The genre that quotes says what a quotation bridge may carry. A subheading standing over a quotation is outside the quotation bridge and is governed by this section.

## Getting there

Settle the reader and the angle before wording anything. Then write three to five variants and keep the clearest, which is rarely the cleverest. Word a subheading from its whole section, once the section is written, in words its first sentence does not use, and leave a quotation standing under it the judgement, figure or concession it is there to carry.
# Headlines — review guidance

Read under [Headlines](headlines.md). Read the text first and say its angle to yourself in one sentence. Then read the headline against that sentence, and each subheading against its own section and against any quotation standing under it, and ask four questions of each. Can every word in it be supported by the text? Is the core message there? Does the tone match the seriousness of the content? Would the reader feel misled afterwards?

## Avoid

Each of these in a headline or a subheading is a finding where you can name what a reader of that heading loses, and no finding where you cannot. A reader loses something where the heading claims more than the text, or something other than it; is louder in tone than the text; says again, in substance, what stands under it; gives away the point of a quotation under it; is a bare label or subject where the text has an angle, or a question where the text answers it; uses words the audience does not know; or leaves a reader who sees only the heading unable to tell what the text is about. Those are instances of the test and not the whole of it, so an item they do not name is still a finding wherever the test holds, as where a colon in place of a verb leaves the reader unable to tell who did what. A loss is something the reader gets wrong or does not get: what the text claims, how seriously it speaks, what it is about, a quotation's point met fresh. - Claims, figures, names or conclusions not found in the text. A headline that sharpens, generalises or draws a conclusion the text itself does not draw is always a finding, however well it reads.
- Vague or mysterious wording that requires reading the text to understand the headline.
- A subject named with nothing said about it, where the text has an angle to state.
- Words, names and abbreviations the audience will not know.
- Partial quotes, colons in place of a verb, stilted headline-speak.
- Puns and references that fail for anyone who does not get the allusion.
- Question headlines. Where the text gives the answer, the headline gives it too. The exceptions are a text built as questions and answers, where the form is natural, and a text that truly leaves the question open, where the headline is deliberately kept from asserting anything.

Name what the reader loses, and repair by rewriting the headline alone, from the text's angle and at the text's own strength. The text stays as it is. A headline or a subheading a round changed is reported with this finding — the part, and the defect that licensed the change — and, where the new one asserts something the old did not, with what it now asserts, so that a reader of the account can tell a repaired part from a rewritten one. A repair keeps the text's recurring words and figures and its meaning: a word or an image the text returns to comes back in the form the text gives it, and the heading names the text's point in the text's own word for it, never in a neighbouring word that widens or shifts what the text says.

## Leave alone

A working headline is left alone. Plain is no defect, and neither is a headline with no number or place where none carries the message, direct address in an instructional text, or an angle other than the one you would have chosen where the text supports it. A label on a reference or navigation text is correct as a label.

Read a heading as its reader meets it, and count a loss that reader would suffer, not one that the strictest reading of a single word could construct. A reader who sees only the heading, as a headline in a list or a search result, has nothing else, so a headline alone has to tell that reader what the text is about. A subheading is met after the headline and the standfirst, so a word or a name they have introduced is known to its reader, and a subheading that refers back to one is not unclear. Four kinds of heading are working, and no *Avoid* item makes one a finding by its wording alone. None of the four overrides the first *Avoid* item, a claim the text does not support as a reader would take it, or the item on a subheading that pre-spends a quotation standing under it:

- An allusion or an image that still tells a reader who sees only the heading what the text is about. It names the text's subject, and may name it in general terms where the text's first lines give the particulars. One that names no subject at all leaves its reader unable to tell what the text is about, however soon the body resolves it, and that is a finding.
- A figure of speech in the text's own register, or the writer's own voice in a signed text, first person included. A figure is an overclaim only where a reader would take it as a factual claim the text does not support, and there the first *Avoid* item decides; an *everything*, a *nothing* or a *never* that overstates in the way the figure means to is read as the figure it is.
- A subheading that states what its section says, where the section's point is not a quotation's judgement, figure or concession. A subheading that sums up its section says what the section says as a whole; that is its work, not a repeat, and it may name the section's limit or its setting rather than its most favourable result. Where the section's point is a quotation's judgement, figure or concession, a subheading that states that point pre-spends the quotation and stays a finding.
- A heading that shares names or topic words with the sentence under it while saying something that sentence does not. A repeat is a finding by what it says again, not by the words it shares.

Where you would word a working heading differently but can name no loss, record nothing against it: a note that it could be better is not a finding, and it licenses no change.

A subheading over a quotation that names the subject, the occasion or the speaker and leaves the quotation its point is working too, and not a subject named with nothing said about it.

===== composition sv
Swedish is a V2 language: the finite verb is the second constituent of a main clause, so fronting anything at all pushes the subject behind the verb. Write *I morgon åker vi till Malmö*, never *I morgon vi åker till Malmö*. This is the single most common structural tell of a text drafted in English and rendered into Swedish.

Compounds are written as one word. *Kvalitetssäkring*, *kundtjänstmedarbetare*, *miljökonsekvensbeskrivning*. Splitting them is not a stylistic choice in Swedish and often changes the meaning outright — *en rökfri miljö* and *en rök fri miljö* are different claims. Where a compound grows unreadably long, rewrite it into a prepositional phrase rather than splitting it.

Definiteness is marked twice. An adjective before a definite noun takes both the front article and the noun's suffix: *den nya rapporten*, *det stora huset*, *de svenska kunderna*. English has one article and drafts translated from it routinely lose one of the two Swedish markers.

The s-passive is the ordinary Swedish passive and is shorter than its periphrastic alternative: *rapporten skickas på fredag*, not *rapporten blir skickad på fredag*. Both exist; the s-form is the unmarked one, and the *bli*-form carries a change-of-state reading that is often not intended.

*Du* is the default address in Swedish prose, including business and journalism. *Ni* to a single reader is either archaic or a deliberate distancing, and reads as a translation from a language that has a formal pronoun.

*Man* is a fallback rather than the ordinary generic pronoun. It is justified where the agent genuinely is anybody at all or is genuinely unknown, and where naming one would claim more than the material carries. Where the sentence has a real subject to hand — the reader, the writer, the organisation, the profession, the study — that subject is what the sentence takes. A text that reaches for *man* with any of those available reads as evasive, and it is usually where an English draft's *you*, *we*, or passive has landed rather than anything the writer chose.

Speech that the text reports is ordinarily set with a speech dash rather than in quotation marks: an interview answer, a remark at a meeting, anything a person said that the text renders readable. A writer reaches for quotation marks where the phrasing itself is the point — where it is what is new, where it is disputed, or where the text is about how the thing was said. What each of the two marks promises a reader, and what that makes each of them a claim about, is settled in Mechanics; this scope says only which one an ordinary Swedish text reaches for first.

Genitive takes a bare *s* with no apostrophe: *Kntnts kunder*, *Sveriges riksdag*. A name already ending in *s*, *x*, or *z* takes nothing at all: *Anders bok*, *Marx teori*.

Swedish tolerates a shorter sentence than English does and punishes subordination harder. Prefer a main clause with a fronted adverbial to a long relative construction, and prefer a verb to a nominalisation: *när kommunen beslutade* over *vid kommunens beslutsfattande*.

Reach for the established Swedish term where one exists and the field actually uses it — *återkoppling*, *underlag*, *avstämning* — but do not purge the loanwords a professional reader expects. A text that writes *dator* and *webbplats* naturally is Swedish; a text that hunts down every English term and replaces it with a coinage nobody says is not.

Read for särskrivning first. A split compound is the error a Swedish reader notices before anything else, and generated or dictated text produces them in bulk.

Check the word order of every clause that opens with something other than the subject. A fronted adverbial, object, or subordinate clause must be followed immediately by the finite verb.

Nominal style is the characteristic failure of Swedish institutional prose. *Genomförande av en utvärdering av verksamheten* is three nouns doing the work of one verb; *utvärdera verksamheten* says it. Look for *-ande*, *-ning*, and *-else* nouns paired with a colourless verb — *ske*, *utföra*, *genomföra*, *möjliggöra* — and give the sentence its real verb back.

Empty attribution: *studier visar*, *experter menar*, *det är allmänt känt att*, with nobody named. In Swedish as in any language, an unattributed authority is a claim the writer has not made.

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

A block quotation is marked by being set off, and that setting is the whole of the mark. Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. A source named with a block sits outside the quotation and after it; set inside, the attribution reads as something the source wrote about itself.

Reported speech is punctuated as a run-in quotation is, and what the setting adds is the layout that says who is speaking. A turn belongs to one speaker and takes a paragraph of its own, and a second speaker beginning inside the first speaker's paragraph is read as the first speaker still talking, however plainly the words belong to somebody else. Where one speaker's turn runs across more than one paragraph, the continuation is marked as the same turn, because a reader shown nothing takes the second paragraph for somebody else's turn: a new paragraph is what a change of speaker looks like in this setting. How a language marks the continuation is its own — a turn left unclosed until its last paragraph, a speech mark opening every one of them — but that the reader can tell one continued turn from two is not the language's to settle.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

## Established variants

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. Only inconsistency within one text is corrected, and it is corrected towards whichever of the established forms that text already uses more.

That preserves nothing the rules in hand name as an error. A construction this contract or the resolved language's own mechanics guidance identifies as wrong is corrected however consistently the text commits to it, because consistency is what an established variant is judged by and never what makes something established. A text that is wrong the same way throughout is wrong throughout.
